variants.name: NestJS interceptor chain (NestInterceptor + CallHandler)
variants.idiom_name: @Injectable() class implements NestInterceptor { intercept(ctx, next: CallHandler): Observable<T> }
variants.implementation_notes: NestJS formalises the pattern as interceptors: `intercept(context, next)` receives a `CallHandler` whose `handle()` invokes the rest of the chain - the next interceptor or the route handler - and returns an `Observable`, so a link either calls `next.handle()` and transforms the stream or skips it to short-circuit (a cache interceptor returning `of(cached)` never runs the route). Binding order via `@UseInterceptors` and the DI container replace the handler factory, and `NestInterceptor<T, R>` is the typed handler contract.
pitfalls: An interceptor that never calls next.handle() silently cancels the route - intended for caches, a bug everywhere else.
The returned Observable must be subscribed or returned; forgetting to return from intercept() leaves the request hanging.
Global interceptors registered through useGlobalInterceptors() cannot inject dependencies; register APP_INTERCEPTOR in a module instead.

variants.name: Typed function chain (framework-free)
variants.idiom_name: type Handler<T> = (req: T) => Result<T> | undefined, walked in an array
variants.implementation_notes: Framework-free TypeScript expresses the pattern with a typed handler alias and an array: a handler returns its result or `undefined` to forward, and the dispatcher walks the array until one returns a value. Type parameters replace the abstract Handler class, and putting an explicit `unhandled` variant in the result union makes the terminal outcome type-checked, so the compiler enforces the part the classic pattern leaves to convention. The Express middleware type is the same shape with a `next` callback instead of a return value.
pitfalls: Using undefined as the forward sentinel forbids handlers that legitimately produce undefined; prefer a discriminated union.
Async handlers need a separate Promise-returning chain type; mixing the two produces accidental thenable results.
Widening the handler alias to any at a registration site silently drops the contract, so export and reuse the alias.
